brief:
Review explanation

How a line's errors build up the mean squared error

interactive
Let me change a line's slope and intercept and see how far six points are from its predictions. Show how each error contributes to the mean squared error.

Presentation
Static
Steps
Over time
Experiment

You will see six fixed data points on a grid and a straight line, with a vertical segment from each point to the line showing its error, and a square drawn on each segment whose area is that error squared. Next to the plot, six bars show each squared error's share of the total, and the mean squared error is written out as the average of those six squares. When you change the slope or the intercept, the line tilts or shifts, the segments and squares grow or shrink, and the bars and the total update right away. This shows that squaring makes large misses count much more than small ones, so one far-off point can dominate the total. You can adjust the slope and intercept to find the line with the smallest mean squared error, and select any point to highlight its error, its square and its share of the total.

ASSUMPTIONS 2
LIMITATIONS 3

findings.message: The x-axis tick label '5' is crossed by point 5's vertical error segment at x=260, and point 2's square's bottom edge (y≈450) runs through it, so the label is hard to read.
The large squares are clipped at the plot edge and overlap each other heavily, so you can't compare their areas by eye. The bars still show the shares.
Point 3's square has its top edge at y≈438, right against the top of the x-axis tick label '5'. Many squares also overlap below the x-axis in a crowded area.

manifest.title: How a line's errors build up the mean squared error
manifest.summary: Six fixed points and a line you control. Each vertical segment is a point's error (actual minus prediction). The square beside it has an area proportional to that error squared. Bars on the right show each square's share of the total. The mean squared error (MSE) is the average of the six squared errors. Change the slope or intercept to see big misses dominate, and look for the smallest MSE.
assumptions: The six data points are fixed example values that lie roughly along a line.
Error is measured vertically: actual y minus the line's predicted y.
Both axes use the same scale (40 pixels per unit). Each square's side is half its error's length, so its area is one quarter of the error squared on that scale and stays proportional to it.
Lines and squares outside the plot area are cut off at its edge, but the numbers on the right always use the full values.
manifest.description: Left: a plot with six dots labelled 1 to 6 and a straight prediction line. A vertical segment joins each dot to the line. A translucent square starts at each dot and grows toward the line, with sides half as long as the segment. Right: the line's equation, then six rows. Each row gives a point's error, its square and its percentage of the total, with a horizontal bar whose length is that percentage. Below the rows, the MSE formula and its value are written out as the sum of the six squares divided by 6. A selector highlights one point's segment, square and bar.
